sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: We introduce Faithfulness Video Score (FVSCORE), a neuro-symbolic framework for specification-driven video generation evaluation. Existing evaluators rely on holistic MLLM judgments or vision-language metrics, yet aligning their scores with human judgments and tracing them to specific temporal violations remain open challenges. FVSCORE addresses these limitations by compiling each video into explicit propositions capturing prompt requirements and implicit propositions capturing unstated physical, temporal, and cross-modal constraints. It grounds each proposition using specialized perceptual tools and evaluates the resulting confidence traces with soft temporal operators inspired by Linear Temporal Logic. A Significance-Aware Calibration step then aligns verification with human perception by retaining only perceptually significant violations before producing a timestamp- and evidence-grounded report. We conduct extensive experiments across public and complex multi-event benchmarks with the strongest video models to date, demonstrating that FVSCORE outperforms holistic and agent-based evaluators in human correlation while providing highly accurate and interpretable feedback.

sections.content: FVScore: Specification-Driven Neuro-Symbolic Video Evaluation Do Xuan Long1 2 *, Long T. Le1, Yiwen Song1, Min-Yen Kan2, Tomas Pfister1 and Yale Song1 1Google Cloud AI Research, 2National University of Singapore We introduce Faithfulness Video Score (FVScore), neuro-symbolic framework for specification-driven video generation evaluation. Existing evaluators rely on holistic MLLM judgments or visionlanguage metrics, yet aligning their scores with human judgments and tracing them to specific temporal violations remain open challenges. FVScore addresses these limitations by compiling each video into explicit propositions capturing prompt requirements and implicit propositions capturing unstated physical, temporal, and cross-modal constraints. It grounds each proposition using specialized perceptual tools and evaluates the resulting confidence traces with soft temporal operators inspired by Linear Temporal Logic. Perception-Aware Calibration step then aligns verification with human perception by retaining only perceptually significant violations before producing timestampand evidence-grounded report. We conduct extensive experiments across public and complex multi-event benchmarks with the strongest video models to date, demonstrating that FVScore outperforms holistic and agent-based evaluators in human correlation while providing more accurate and interpretable feedback. 1. Introduction Automatic video evaluation is central yet unresolved problem in generative AI. As text-to-video (T2V) models (ByteDance Seed, 2026; Google Deepmind, 2025) attain increasingly outstanding visual realism, judging generation primarily by visual quality is no longer sufficient. generated video can look sharp and cinematic, yet appear nonsensical to human viewers at the same time. For example, video may misbind requested action (textvideo alignment), lose character identity over time (temporal consistency), violate basic physical laws (physical commonsense), or desynchronize audio from its visual source (videoaudio alignment) (Guo et al., 2025; Sharan et al., 2025; Tilak et al., 2026; Zheng et al., 2025b). Together, these constitute the essential dimensions of faithful generation. Evaluating them requires determining not only explicit user requirements, but also implicit commonsense behaviors that humans expect. Figure 1 Three paradigms for video evaluation. Metric suites score predefined dimensions, while MLLM judges produce reasoning reports. FVScore compiles explicit and video-conditioned implicit propositions, evaluates their confidence traces, and reports dimension scores with timestamped evidence. Existing studies have addressed important parts of this challenge. Early metrics compare distributional or joint-embedding features (Hessel et al., 2021; Unterthiner et al., 2018) for textvideo alignment, while comprehensive benchmarks such as VBench, EvalCrafter, and T2VScore evaluate videos using criteria-based proxies (Huang et al., 2024; Corresponding author(s): Do Xuan Long: xuanlong.do@u.nus.edu; Long T. Le, Yale Song: {longtle, yalesong}@google.com * This work was done while Do Xuan Long was Student Researcher at Google Cloud AI Research. Our project is available at this url. FVScore: Specification-Driven Neuro-Symbolic Video Evaluation Liu et al., 2024; Sun et al., 2025). Because such metrics can align weakly with human ratings and offer limited interpretability, recent approaches train evaluators directly on human scores (He et al., 2024, 2025), use MLLM-based multi-agent critiques for better interpretability (Chen et al., 2024; Long et al., 2026a,b), or decompose prompts into atomic visual checks (Cho et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2023; Sharan et al., 2025; Song et al., 2026) (Figure 1). Nevertheless, they remain limited by predefined evaluation criteria or user input requirements. To our knowledge, no evaluator explicitly derives which implicit temporal constraints emerge from video events, nor accurately verifies when they are violated. Consequently, perceptually salient violations, such as implausible state transitions or videoaudio mismatches, are often missed or folded into holistic scores, yielding diagnoses too general to identify what failed and when. To address these limitations, we formulate video evaluation as Specification-Driven Verification. Inspired by formal verification (Baier et al., 2008; Pnueli, 1977), we use specification languages to evaluate videos on specific faithfulness constraints, enabling targeted failure localization. We introduce FVScore, neuro-symbolic framework that separates this process into compilation and execution. The compiler generates explicit propositions from the user prompt and implicit propositions from observed video dynamics. During execution, FVScore routes these to specialized neural or symbolic verifiers operating over temporally indexed video representation. It then evaluates their confidence traces using soft LTL-inspired operators to identify what fails and when. Finally, Perception-Aware Calibration step retains perceptually significant violations to align scores with humans and produce timestamp-grounded diagnoses. Our comprehensive evaluations show that FVScore significantly outperforms existing evaluators, increasing human correlation by up to 17% on alignment, 26% on physical commonsense, 20% in consistency, and 44% on videoaudio sync, alongside 55% and 50% average win margins in groundedness and completeness of the feedback. In summary, our contributions are: We formulate video evaluation as Specification-Driven Verification, deriving both explicit (prompt-stated) and implicit (video-conditioned) requirements for faithfulness video evaluation. We introduce FVScore, an automatic framework that compiles these requirements into propositions, routes them to specialized verifiers, evaluates their confidence traces, and calibrates scores for human alignment. FVScore achieves significantly stronger human alignment than prior evaluators (e.g., 26% and 44% correlation gains on physical commonsense and videoaudio sync) while providing more grounded and useful diagnoses. 2. Related Work Generative Video Evaluation. Automatic video evaluation has achieved remarkable progress, developed along four lines. Earlier efforts develop distribution and similarity metrics (Hessel et al., 2021; Heusel et al., 2017; Salimans et al., 2016), but reduce video quality or textvideo alignment to single scalar. Extending them, benchmark suites cover comprehensive dimensions (Hua et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2024, 2025; Liu et al., 2023, 2024; Sun et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2026), yet aligning their scores to human judgments remains significant challenge (Sharan et al., 2025). To improve it, recent work trains specialized evaluators directly on human ratings (Bansal et al., 2025, 2026; He et al., 2024, 2025; Liu et al., 2026) or employs MLLMs as judges (Chen et al., 2024; Long et al., 2026a,b; Zheng et al., 2023); nevertheless, their evaluation remains unstable across models, scenarios, and rubric choices. Recent methods decompose the prompt into atomic verifications (Cho et al., 2024; Guan et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2023; Song et al., 2026), leading to more interpretable evaluation. Closest to us, NeuS-V (Sharan et al., 2025) verifies textvideo alignment through formal verification. 2 FVScore: Specification-Driven Neuro-Symbolic Video Evaluation However, we find that it correlates weakly with human judgments on public benchmarks, as it can compound joint probabilities over frames (Section 4), remains restricted to single criterion, and produces no grounded explanation. FVScore instead provides unified interface that verifies both explicit and implicit propositions over temporal video representation. This allows it to identify what fails and when, providing more interpretable and aligned evaluation while can be readily extended to future evaluation criteria. Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning. Neuro-symbolic reasoning bridges the gap between neural networks pattern recognition and formal logics interpretability (Hu et al., 2016; Lu et al., 2024; Mao et al., 2019; Yi et al., 2018; Yu et al., 2023). These methods separate perception from reasoning: neural front-end turns visual evidence into structured representation over which symbolic back-end reasons, whether through learned program execution (Mao et al., 2019; Yi et al., 2018) or training-free program synthesis (Gupta and Kembhavi, 2023; Surís et al., 2023). This paradigm has been extended to video through spatio-temporal causal reasoning benchmarks (Yi et al., 2019), and recently to text video alignment by NeuS-V (Sharan et al., 2025), which compiles the prompt into temporal-logic specification and verifies it against probabilistic video automaton. However, its automaton grows exponentially with propositions, and calculating satisfaction as joint probability over-penalizes videos as more frames are evaluated. Furthermore, NeuS-V derives logical programs from prompt only. In contrast, FVScore dynamically generates implicit propositions from the video itself. By verifying each proposition independently against its own confidence trace, FVScore prevents single failure from artificially depressing the overall score. 3. Methodology 3.1. Problem Formulation Given video 𝑉 synthesized from diffusion model using natural-language prompt 𝑃, our goal is to evaluate its faithfulness. Following recent literature, we define faithfulness across four essential dimensions: textvideo alignment (Huang et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024; Sun et al., 2025), physical commonsense (Bansal et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2025), temporal consistency (Tilak et al., 2026; Zheng et al., 2025b), and videoaudio synchronization (Hua et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2026). In addition, it is worth noting that while textvideo alignment is evaluated against requirements explicitly stated in prompt 𝑃, the remaining dimensions rely on implicit physical and causal constraints dictated by the specific events generated in 𝑉. An ideal evaluator therefore must dynamically derive both these explicit and implicit requirements and judge them in alignment with humans. Specification-Driven Verification. We formulate video evaluation as Specification-Driven Verification, in which the evaluator first compiles set of situation-specific specifications Φ and then verifies them against perceptual evidence and generates the report. Unlike holistic evaluators, Φ is not predefined; instead, it is situation-dependent and derived from the prompt and video. 3 FVScore: Specification-Driven Neuro-Symbolic Video Evaluation Figure 2 FVScore, which compiles the user prompt and video observations into explicit and implicit propositions, verifies them via specialized neural and symbolic tools, and applies Perception-Aware Calibration to produce timestamp-grounded scores and reports. 3.2. The FVScore Framework Figure 2 outlines our proposed FVScore which leverages Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) as the core engine. It realizes 𝑆 through Compilation phase that produces the specification Φ and an Execution phase that verifies it and generates the report. Compilation occurs in two steps: Step 1 derives explicit propositions from 𝑃, while Step 3 derives implicit propositions from representation constructed in Step 2. Execution then verifies each proposition to obtain its score (Step 4), then identifies perceptually significant violations, aggregates dimension scores, and produces grounded report (Step 5). Unified Specification Representation. We design unified representation where every requirement from all dimensions is compiled into proposition 𝜙𝑖 = ( 𝑝𝑖, 𝜏𝑖, 𝜔𝑖). This encapsulates an atomic predicate 𝑝𝑖, Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) operator 𝜏𝑖 {Always, Eventually, Until}, and verification route 𝜔𝑖. The route dispatches the predicate to the appropriate grounding track (either neural or graph; detailed in Step 4) and verification tool, which yields confidence trace over the video. The 4 FVScore: Specification-Driven Neuro-Symbolic Video Evaluation temporal operator then reduces this trace into single proposition score. To verify temporal visual states within the video, we construct an ordered sequence of per-keyframe scene graphs = {𝐺𝑘}𝐾 . Each 𝐺𝑘 records entity-state assignments and 𝑘=1 action relations inferred from the corresponding keyframe and constrained to V. The graph can also be augmented with tool-specific relation and attribute evidence, such as depth ordering and shot scale. Details of graph construction and the associated perceptual tools are provided in Section D.1. Audio Layer. For video with an audio stream, we extract mono waveform and apply specialized audio and MLLM tools (Google, 2025; Park et al., 2024) to identify foreground sound events, each represented by its start time, end time, description, and confidence. When Φexp contains auditory propositions, their predicate texts are supplied as the target sound vocabulary. The audio layer is empty when no audio stream is available. Step 3. Implicit Proposition Compilations. This step expands Φ with implicit propositions Φimp that capture unstated commonsense, consistency, and cross-modal requirements. 5 FVScore: Specification-Driven Neuro-Symbolic Video Evaluation Physical Commonsense Propositions Φphy imp. To extract the unstated physical constraints implied by the videos dynamics, we first convert the entity-state sequence in into an event-transition narrative by retaining only the state dimensions that change across keyframes. Nevertheless, extracting the implicit physical rules that govern this narrative sequence is challenging. Because the space of possible rules is open-ended, naively prompting an MLLM tends to produce many trivial or redundant rules, overshadowing those violations that actually matter to human perception. To systematically discover those that matter most to humans, motivated by the Temporal-Property Hierarchy Theory (Manna and Pnueli, 1990), FVScore generates physical propositions across four core categories: (i) Invariants, which enforce persistent constraints such as mutual exclusion and count stability; (ii) Causality, which requires an enabling cause to be present when its effect occurs; and (iii) Liveness, which requires physical process that has started to reach its expected completion. We additionally generate (iv) Plausibility propositions for plausible entity appearance, layout, and sounds. Each proposition is strictly assigned to one category to avoid duplication, while prompt restatements and trivial rules are excluded: imp Compileimp Φphy MLLM(𝑃, E, V, 𝐺, Ω) (5) Consistency Propositions Φcons imp . For each entity in E, we define template-based proposition by requiring its identity or layout to remain coherent across keyframes while permitting natural changes in pose, motion, tone, or lighting. separate proposition enforces global background stability, explicitly prohibiting abrupt scene cuts, objects that inexplicably appear or vanish, and temporal flickering. Synchronization Propositions Φsync imp . For each detected foreground sound event in R, we define template-based proposition requiring the sound to be temporally synchronized with the visual content during its detected interval. Each proposition retains the sound description and its start and end times, which is then evaluated with the corresponding video segment for synchronization. 3.2.2. Execution Step 4. Neural-Symbolic Proposition Verifications. This step verifies Φ to produce the scores and reasoning. Neural Predicate Grounding. For each 𝜙𝑖 Φ routed for neural verification, we ground its atomic predicate 𝑝𝑖 in visual evidence using either an MLLM or specialized neural models. Depending on the property, both explicit and implicit propositions are evaluated against discrete keyframes (e.g., for static entity presence and counting) or continuous video segments (e.g., for motion), producing frame-level confidence scores. Consistency yields per-entity and background scores over the ordered keyframes, while videoaudio sync yields per-sound synchronization scores from the associated muted video segments. Each dimension retains its own score representation for subsequent aggregation. Graph Predicate Grounding. For propositions routed to graph-based grounding, we compile their predicates into formal queries using the MLLM, strictly grounded on V, and evaluate them against scene graph G. The query language represents entity presence and subject relations using Exists and ExistsEdge, and composes multiple conditions using And and Or. Together, the neural and graph-based routes provide each proposition with confidence trace for symbolic verification. Symbolic Verification. We next evaluate the confidence traces using the temporal operators 𝜏𝑖. Unlike prior methods (Sharan et al., 2025) that compute joint probabilities over video automata, which scales exponentially with the number of propositions and whose joint-probability computation can compound uncertainty as more frames and propositions are evaluated, we verify each proposition FVScore: Specification-Driven Neuro-Symbolic Video Evaluation independently using soft LTL-inspired operators: Always averages confidence over the full video or its specified temporal window, Eventually retains the maximum confidence, and Until tracks the minimum confidence that the preceding predicate holds or occurs before the consequent occurs, while checking any specified response delay or repetition requirement. We apply temporal tolerance of 𝑡 = 0.1s for strict timing constraints like windows or deadlines, yielding score 𝑠𝑖 for each proposition 𝜙𝑖 Φ𝑑 for dim 𝑑, which are then passed to the next step for perceptual calibration and dimension aggregation. Step 5. Calibration and Report. While proposition scores provide useful insights into video faithfulness, they do not explicitly account for the perceptual significance of individual violations, which limits their alignment with human judgments. We introduce PAC, simple proposition-level Perception-Aware Calibration mechanism for alignment. We employ many-shot in-context MLLM adjudicator to assign each proposition and its score binary weight according to whether violating it would be perceptually significant to humans (𝑤𝑖 = 1) or negligible noise (𝑤𝑖 = 0). To construct this many-shot context, we sample violated propositions from highly rated and poorly rated videos as negligible noise and perceptually significant demonstrations respectively from held-out set. We then cap the maximum demonstrations (20 each type). After obtaining 𝑤𝑖, defining Φ 𝑑 = {𝜙𝑖 Φ𝑑 : 𝑤𝑖 = 1}, the final score for dim 𝑑 is: score𝑑 = Agg𝑑 (cid:0){ 𝑠𝑖 : 𝜙𝑖 Φ 𝑑 }(cid:1), (6) where Agg𝑑 aggregates the proposition scores relevant to each dimension, with Agg𝑑 () := 1. We implement Agg as the average; PAC can either increase or decrease aggregated scores. Finally, FVScore synthesizes natural-language Evaluation Report from the PAC-filtered propositions, summarizing what succeeded and failed and grounding every claim in specific propositions, verification rationales, and timestamps (in seconds). 4. Experiments We conduct extensive experiments to answer five key research questions: (RQ1) Does our neurosymbolic approach improve alignment with human judgements compared to existing evaluators? (RQ2) Does proposition-level decomposition yield more accurate, grounded, and useful qualitative feedback? (RQ3) How do specific symbolic verification tools and temporal logic operators contribute to the frameworks overall performance? (RQ4) How accurately does the compiler generate and orchestrate explicit and implicit propositions across specialized verification tools? (RQ5) To what extent does PAC successfully filter imperceptible noise to align strict formal verification with human perception? 4.1. Experimental Setups Baselines. We compare FVScore against seven video evaluators grouped into four widely used paradigms. (i) Evaluation Suites: VBench (Huang et al., 2024), standard comprehensive suite for video generation evaluation. (ii) Advanced MLLM Reasoning: Methods that enhance MLLM reasoning, including MLLM-Judge w/ Self-Consistency (Wang et al., 2023); Self-Refine (Madaan et al., 2023), which iteratively generates and incorporates its own critiques up to 10 iterations; and Multi-Agent Debate (Du et al., 2024), where multiple MLLM instances debate to reach consensus score up to 10 rounds. (iii) Agentic Frameworks: VISTAs MMAC (Long et al., 2026b), jury of specialized agents scoring along visual, audio, and contextual dimensions; and VQQA (Song et al., 2026), question-answering evaluator that scores via prompt-derived queries. (iv) Neuro-Symbolic Methods: NeuS-V (Sharan et al., 2025), temporal-logic evaluation method targeting textvideo alignment. We evaluate FVScore on two primary objectives: score alignment with human judgments and qualitative feedback quality. To ensure comprehensiveness, we test across both singleevent and complex multi-event scenarios. For single-event evaluation, we sample 900 prompts with per-video human ratings from EvalCrafter (Liu et al., 2024), VideoFeedback (He et al., 2024), and VideoFeedback2 (He et al., 2025) (300 prompts each). For complex scenarios, we include VBench 2.0 (Zheng et al., 2025a), which contains 320 multi-step prompts requiring coherent sequential ordering. However, because VBench 2.0 lacks per-video human ratings, it can only be used to evaluate feedback quality. Furthermore, it lacks the dense causality, strict response deadlines, and cross-modal constraints required to stress-test the faithfulness. To bridge these gaps, we introduce FVBench, testing benchmark that features 200 compositional prompts with: (i) Cross-modal multi-event instructions: dense scenarios mapped to classical temporal properties; and (ii) Very high-quality videos: 400 videos synthesized by SOTA video models (ByteDance Seed, 2026; Google Deepmind, 2025). Our construction details are outlined in Section D.3. We provide an end-to-end example of FVScore in our supplementary materials. Metrics. For correlations, following Sharan et al. (2025), we measure Pearson (𝑃) and Spearman (𝑆) rank correlation against human ratings across FVBench, EvalCrafter, VideoFeedback, and VideoFeedback2 (for available dimensions). For feedback quality, we conduct pairwise report comparisons on FVBench and VBench 2.0 using Gemini 3.1 Pro (Google, 2026). Given the video and two anonymized reports, the judge assigns win/tie/loss/Δ=win-loss outcomes based on (1) Accuracy (factual correctness to the video), (2) Groundedness (attribution to specific, observable moments), (3) Completeness (coverage of prompt requirements), and (4) Helpfulness (clarity in explaining failure modes without rewarding verbosity), with report order swapped to mitigate positional bias. Our tables also show that PAC notably improves correlations on nearly all dimensions, confirming the importance of calibrating violations. Holistic MLLMs degrade notably on multi-event scenarios, failing to track conditional exceptions, invariants, bounded deadlines, and multimodal synchronization. On EvalCrafter and VideoFeedback2, we find that all baselines achieve 0.600.70 Pearson correlation on textvideo alignment. For EvalCrafters single-event prompts, MLLM baselines perform nearly on par with FVScore, while VISTA even surpasses it on consistency because its adversarial critique can identify issues in short videos without further decomposition. Meanwhile, on FVBench the baselines fall to only 0.330.41(𝑃). Our human investigation shows that holistic evaluators struggle with dense multi-event prompts requiring temporal logic, particularly those that involve conditional exceptions, repeated-instance constraints, global invariants, and response deadlines (e.g., actions required unless, for each instance, whenever, or within period). See Section for some of our case studies. FVScore demonstrates robustness across evaluation dimensions. When analyzing human scores, we notice that their distributions naturally vary across dimensions. For example, on FVBench (Figure 4), human ratings for temporal consistency and audiovisual synchronization are quite high because SOTA video generation models already excel on them, whereas textvideo alignment and physical commonsense remain challenging. We observe that existing baselines struggle to adapt to these different distributions, revealing several noticeable behavior biases. For example, MLLM evaluators tend to flatten scores across bins, VBench saturates when evaluating SOTA video models, and NeuS-V concentrates scores in the 0.00.2 bins. For NeuS-V, this bias comes from applying strict LTL operators, such as multiplying confidences across frames for ALWAYS. This formulation is brittle, as localized MLLM error can collapse the final score, especially when evaluating many frames (doubling the #frames drops Pearson to 0.1 on both FVBench and EvalCrafter). By using our soft LTL-inspired operators, FVScore prevents localized errors from dominating and better matches human-rating distributions across dimensions. Table 3 averages our results over all dimensions and benchmarks. We observe that the average Δ over baselines is largest on Groundedness and Completeness. For example, FVScore is more grounded than the baselines on FVBench when comparing physical commonsense reports with Δ = +55.4%  (Table 14)  . It is also more complete with Δ = +57.8% when comparing text-video alignment reports  (Table 12)  . Through manual investigation, we observe that holistic evaluators tend to focus on scene-level events while often overlooking localized artifacts. For example, when prompt requires guard to tap badge to enter corridor, holistic evaluators often recognize that the guard enters the corridor, yet may overlook the ordering error if the door opens slightly before the badge is tapped. Because FVScore evaluates these implicit requirements as isolated propositions, it can reliably capture the error in time. In addition, FVScore also achieves substantial gains in Accuracy and Helpfulness with average Δ more than 30%, further demonstrating the quality of its diagnostic reports. We provide more examples in our supplementary materials. FVScores reports excel further as scenarios encode more complex temporal constraints. Similar to our previous observations on correlations, our pairwise margins (Δ) increase substantially from VBench 2.0 to FVBench, jumping from +33.2% to +47.9% on alignment and from +10.5% to +50.1% on commonsense. Comparing two datasets, we find that VBench 2.0 prompts primarily require event ordering, which MLLMs and agentic frameworks can often verify well through scene-level reasoning. FVBench, however, introduces more complex temporal constraints (e.g., deadlines, exceptions, invariants), which demand more precise checks. This further consolidates our conclusion that specification-driven approach is essential for evaluating complex temporal and logical dependencies. 5. Analysis 5.1. Ablation Studies (RQ3) We ablate four components of FVScore without PAC. We deliberately isolate the uncalibrated execution engine because applying PAC could obscure the raw effects of the ablations. Specifically, we study: (i) tool routing, comparing our full hybrid engine with Neural-only and Graph-only; (ii) confidence-trace temporal operators, compared with original LTL and no temporal operator (use ALWAYS); (iii) implicit propositions, incrementally adding invariant, causality, and liveness schemes; and (iv) frame sampling, varied by 2x and 4x. Graph-only performs poorly on consistency and commonsense, where we observe frequent false negatives. This is because symbolic queries are bound to the scene graph; any visual details missed during construction evaluate to false. Meanwhile, neural-only remains competitive on simple prompts in VideoFeedback but degrades on the complex multi-event ones in FVBench, highlighting the importance of hybrid verification. We also see that removing temporal operators notably reduces FVBench scores, while the original LTL lowers them further on all metrics. These results highlight the importance of our soft operator design. Implicit propositions improve commonsense evaluation, while denser sampling introduces false violations. Adding invariant, causality, and liveness propositions progressively improves commonsense correlation from 0.188/0.166 to 0.256/0.230 approaching the full models 0.326/0.344. This improvement demonstrates both the importance of these proposition families and the effectiveness of deriving situation-specific constraints for detecting human-perceptible physical failures. In addition, we notice that denser sampling is not always helpful. On VideoFeedback, 4 sampling reduces FVBench alignment to 0.277/0.310 and commonsense to 0.147/0.133. Our manual inspection reveals that oversampling introduces noisy intermediate observations into the scene graph. For example, rapid motion can produce blurred frames in which detectors temporarily lose objects, causing false detected violations. 5.2. Proposition and Routing Analysis (RQ4) We conduct careful human evaluation of proposition quality and tool-routing accuracy. Three highly qualified annotators evaluate propositions from 150 videos sampled across FVBench, VBench 2.0, and VideoFeedback2, rating (i) Faithfulness to the ground-truth prompt or video constraints as binary metric and (ii) Completeness on 15 scale for two sets of explicit and implicit propositions. Another set of three annotators evaluates whether the assigned tool is optimal for 120 routed propositions sampled from FVBench. Proposition compilation and tool routing are highly reliable. Our results are provided in Section C.4. As shown in Tables 9 and 10, explicit propositions achieve 96.0%97.1% faithfulness and 4.454.62 completeness, while implicit propositions achieve 82.6%88.9% and 4.094.56, respectively. The lower implicit scores reflect the open-ended nature of deriving unstated physical constraints, for which annotators may disagree on the necessary rules. Routing achieves 100% correctness for the Shot, Depth, and MLLM tools and 80%94% for Motion and Audio, where general object actions, 11 FVScore: Specification-Driven Neuro-Symbolic Video Evaluation such as throwing ball or playing an instrument, are occasionally routed to the MLLM. While our results are MLLM-specific, they show that compiling videos into formal specifications and routing them to specialized verifiers are highly tractable. 5.3. PAC Analysis (RQ5) We evaluate PAC as both micro-level classifier and macro-level calibrator using 150 PAC-excluded explicit and implicit propositions, labeled by three annotators as either imperceptible artifacts or significant failures. We report PACs F1 and recall against their majority vote, and compare preversus post-calibration score distributions on FVBench. PAC reliably isolates human-salient errors. PAC achieves 85.7% F1 and 90.0% recall, indicating that it rarely filters out genuine generation errors. Studying false cases, we conclude that PACs remaining errors arise from the context-dependent nature of perceptual significance. For example, missing object shadow might be an imperceptible artifact in fast-moving action sequence, but that same violation becomes glaring failure in close-up shot. Additionally, as shown in Figure 5, FVScores uncalibrated scores generally agree with human ratings but tend to over-penalize videos. PAC effectively mitigates this, preserving low scores for flawed videos while restoring high scores for successful ones and shifting the distribution closer to human judgments. 6. Conclusions We introduced FVScore, neural-symbolic specification-driven video evaluation framework that compiles prompts and videos into explicit and implicit propositions, routes them to specialized neural and graph verifiers, and evaluates their confidence traces using symbolic operators. Across public and complex multi-event benchmarks, FVScore outperforms traditional and agentic baselines in human alignment and diagnostic accuracy, groundedness, completeness, and helpfulness. These results establish proposition-level verification as robust foundation for more human-aligned and interpretable video evaluation.

Case Studies We provide two qualitative examples comparing FVScore to the plain MLLM baseline illustrating how it works in Figure 3. As seen in the warehouse scenario (Figure 3, Top), the baseline MLLM assigns perfect 1.00 for physical commonsense, overlooking severe micro-level errors like the mechanical arm missing the box and the object flipping and unnaturally changing size by the end. By decomposing the scene into explicit and implicit propositions, FVScore successfully catches these localized physical violationsflagging exact errors in object permanence and volume conservationto yield score (0.39) that closely matches human judgment (0.35). Furthermore, explicit proposition tracking prevents failures on strict temporal and cross-modal rules. In the timer scenario (Figure 3, Bottom), the prompt requires monotonic countdown followed by an alarm. While the baseline gives vague, overly forgiving scores, FVScore evaluates precise parametric constraints. It logs the exact sequence breakdown (00 : 02 00 : 01 00 : 05) and drops the audiovideo sync score to 0.00 upon detecting an ungrounded alarm sound, demonstrating vastly superior diagnostic accuracy. 17 FVScore: Specification-Driven Neuro-Symbolic Video Evaluation B. Limitations While FVScore makes substantial progress toward human-aligned video evaluation, several limitations remain that motivate future research. First, our soft temporal operators trade strict logical satisfaction for robustness to perceptual evidence. Although this design improves human correlation in our experiments notably, averaging confidence traces can occasionally underweight localized, catastrophic violations that require strict symbolic verification. Future work could explore adaptive temporal operators and severity-aware aggregation to enforce hard constraints while preserving robustness to frame-level understanding noise. Second, FVScores verification is constrained by the accuracy of its underlying MLLM and perceptual grounding tools during state extraction and predicate verification. However, because FVScore is modular and tool-agnostic, it will naturally benefit as foundation models and specialized perception tools continue to advance. Finally, while PAC effectively filters out perceptually negligible violations using lightweight text-level adjudication, modeling visual contextdependent significance to humans remains an open challenge. Future work could investigate visual-context-aware calibration to better capture nuanced human judgments across diverse scenarios. C. Additional Discussions C.1. Experiments With Other MLLMs Table 5 evaluates whether FVScore generalizes across different backbone MLLMs. We experimented with four other SOTA omni models across scales that are capable of understanding videos, namely Qwen3.8-Omni (Team, 2026b), Qwen3.5 (9B, 27B) (Team, 2026a) and MiniMaxM3 (Lai et al., 2026). We observe that all tested backbones produce positive to strong correlations with human judgments across the evaluated dimensions, indicating that the specification-driven framework is not specific to just Gemini models. Gemini 3 Flash nevertheless provides the strongest and most consistent overall performance, particularly on FVBench. Other backbones remain competitive on individual dimensions: Qwen3.5-9B surprisingly achieves the strongest VideoFeedback consistency correlation, Qwen3.5-27B performs best in Pearson correlation on VideoFeedback alignment, and MiniMaxM3 matches Gemini 3 Flash on FVBench physical commonsense. Nevertheless, Qwen3.8-Omni performs strongest across these newly experimented omni models. In addition, PAC generally improves performance across backbones, increasing Pearson correlation in 12 of the 15 non-default backbonedimension settings. However, the gains are not uniform: calibration occasionally reduces correlation, particularly on VideoFeedback alignment and for Qwen3.5-27B on physical commonsense. This variation is expected because PAC relies on the backbones ability to distinguish perceptually significant violations from minor artifacts. Overall, the results demonstrate that FVScore transfers across both openand closed-source MLLMs, while stronger backbone reasoning yields more reliable proposition compilation, verification, and calibration. C.2. Additional Baseline Comparisons In this section, we further compare FVScore with video evaluators trained on human annotations and those specialized for individual evaluation dimensions. We first compare FVScore with VideoScore2 (He et al., 2025), learned video evaluator, on text video alignment and physical commonsense. On VideoFeedback, VideoScore2 slightly outperforms FVScore on alignment, reaching 0.582/0.579 compared with 0.564/0.564. However, on the more complex multi-event videos in FVBench, FVScore substantially outperforms VideoScore2 on both alignment (0.579/0.566 vs. 0.349/0.365) and physical commonsense (0.558/0.528 vs. 0.303/0.289). These results suggest that learned holistic scoring transfers well to simpler public videos but struggles with dense temporal and implicit physical constraints, for which proposition-level verification is particularly beneficial. The ONLY task these evaluators should be doing is: checking whether the VIDEO faithfully depicts what the PROMPT describes. This means verifying presence of described objects, actions, spatial arrangements, temporal ordering, and other explicit prompt requirements. IMPORTANT: Comments about general video quality (artifacts, flickering, deformation, smoothness, resolution, animation quality, cinematic quality) are IRRELEVANT to text-video alignment unless they directly prevent prompt requirement from being recognizable. Do NOT reward an evaluator for pointing out visual defects that have nothing to do with whether the prompt's content is depicted.
